analysis.one_liner: Pauses new mountaintop removal coal mining permits until a federal health study is finished.
analysis.headline: The ACHE Act died without a vote: it was introduced in July 2023 with 14 cosponsors, referred to three House committees, and never advanced before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop federal agencies from issuing or renewing permits for mountaintop removal coal mining in Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Virginia until the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences completes a study on whether the mining harms nearby residents. Mining companies could keep operating existing sites, but they would have to monitor and publicly report water, air, soil, and noise pollution every month, and a one-time fee on mining companies would cover the cost of the study and monitoring.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities near mountaintop removal mining sites in central Appalachia. The bill's stated purpose is to protect them from pollution linked in prior peer-reviewed research to birth defects, chronic lung and heart disease, and elevated mortality while the federal health study runs. Residents would also get searchable public data on pollution from nearby mines.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Appalachian communities near mountaintop removal mines

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans new or renewed federal permits for mountaintop removal projects, or their expansion, until the Secretary of Health and Human Services publishes a determination that the mining poses no health risk to nearby residents.
The National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences must run a comprehensive study of health impacts on people living near mountaintop removal sites and publish the results.

Companies still mining would have to continuously monitor water, air, and noise pollution and periodically monitor soil, then report results monthly to a public, searchable federal database within seven days.

If a company fails to monitor or report, it loses eligibility for any new or renewed federal permit, and a one-time fee on current and past operators covers the federal cost of the study and monitoring.

analysis.who_pays: Mountaintop removal coal companies, which would face a freeze on new, renewed, or expanded permits during the study, new monthly monitoring and reporting costs, and a one-time fee. If a mine expansion or renewal is delayed long enough, some mining jobs in the affected region could be at risk.

drawbacks.text: A permit moratorium lasting as long as the study takes could block mine renewals and expansions and put mining jobs in central Appalachian communities at risk, in a region where coal employment is already declining.
The moratorium is one-sided: it lifts only if the study finds no health risk, meaning even an ambiguous or incomplete study result would leave new permits frozen indefinitely.

The bill does not shut down existing mines; companies could keep operating under current permits with only monitoring and reporting added, so nearby residents get data but not immediate relief from ongoing pollution.
The study is limited to the four steep-slope states named in the bill, so identical mining practices just outside those states would not trigger the moratorium or the monitoring rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents near mountaintop removal sites, the bill offers a credible federal answer to documented health concerns plus real-time pollution data, while leaving current mines open so coal production does not stop outright. The costs fall on a small number of mining companies and, indirectly, on some mining jobs if permit renewals stall. The main design weakness is that the moratorium's exit condition is absolute — the study must find no risk at all — which could stretch the freeze well past the study's completion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, then to two subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, joined by eight original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The Speaker referred it to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, and within a day it was sent to subcommittees in two of them.
No committee ever held a markup, reported the bill, or brought it to the floor, and no version was introduced in the Senate; it died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mountaintop removal coal companies are better off: no study was commissioned, no monitoring requirements or fees were imposed, and new permits kept being issued under the existing rules for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, including the Kentucky sponsor whose own district is affected, and no Republican signed on or acted to move the bill.

industries.note: The bill would freeze their permits for new, renewed, or expanded mines until a health study cleared them, and would impose monthly pollution monitoring, public reporting, and a one-time fee on current and past operators. Because the bill died, they kept operating with none of those requirements.

The moratorium is limited to surface mining with explosives in steep-slope regions of four states, so underground coal mining and mining outside those states would be untouched; the main industry-wide effect would be on permit renewals for mountaintop sites. Coal production from existing mountaintop mines would continue during the study.
A new mandate for continuous water, air, noise, and soil monitoring at every mountaintop removal site would create ongoing demand for pollution monitoring and reporting work.
